Exodus 1.audience: Israel remembered itself as a people once enslaved in Egypt; the law repeatedly reminds them, "ye were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21). This chapter describes how that slavery began.

culture.title: Store cities and brick-making
culture.text: Egyptian kings used forced labor for building projects. Pithom and Raamses were store cities in the eastern Nile Delta. Mud bricks, mixed with straw and dried in the sun, were the standard building material for everything except temples and tombs.

culture.title: Midwives
culture.text: Births were attended by midwives, women skilled in delivery. The text names two of them, Shiphrah and Puah, while the Pharaoh himself remains unnamed.

Exodus 2.audience: Israel knew Moses as the founder of its law and worship. This chapter tells of his birth, his Egyptian upbringing, and his flight to Midian, the region where he would later lead Israel.

culture.title: A papyrus basket
culture.text: Papyrus reeds grew thickly along the Nile and were woven into boats, baskets, and mats, and made into writing material. Moses' basket is sealed with slime (bitumen) and pitch.

culture.title: Raised at court
culture.text: Egyptian royal households raised and educated children, including foreigners. Stephen later says Moses "was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22).

culture.title: Meeting at a well
culture.text: Wells were where shepherds gathered and where travelers met local families—just as Abraham's servant met Rebekah and Jacob met Rachel (Genesis 24:11–15; 29:9–10).

Exodus 3.audience: Horeb, "the mountain of God," is the same mountain where Israel later received the law (Exodus 19:20; Deuteronomy 4:10). Hearers knew God's name revealed here as the name they used in worship.

culture.title: Removing sandals
culture.text: Taking off one's shoes showed respect in a holy place. Priests in Israel served barefoot in the sanctuary, and Joshua is given the same command (Joshua 5:15).

culture.title: Asking for jewels
culture.text: Departing servants or captives receiving goods from their masters echoes Israel's later law, which commanded that a freed slave not be sent away empty (Deuteronomy 15:13–14).

Exodus 4.audience: Aaron, introduced here as Moses' spokesman, was the ancestor of Israel's priests. Hearers knew his descendants as the only ones allowed to serve at the altar (Numbers 18:7).

culture.title: The shepherd's rod
culture.text: A shepherd carried a staff for guiding and protecting the flock. Moses' ordinary rod becomes "the rod of God" (Exodus 4:20).

culture.title: Serpents in Egypt
culture.text: The cobra was a symbol of royal power in Egypt and appears on Pharaoh's crown. A rod becoming a serpent would have had special force in Pharaoh's court.

Exodus 5.audience: Israel's law later required that wages be paid on time and that workers be treated fairly (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Hearers knew what forced labor under harsh taskmasters had been like.

culture.title: Straw in bricks
culture.text: Chopped straw was mixed into mud to make bricks hold together. Forcing the Israelites to gather their own straw while making the same number of bricks greatly increased their labor.

culture.title: Taskmasters and officers
culture.text: Egyptian taskmasters supervised the work, while Israelite officers (foremen) were responsible for their crews' quotas. The officers were beaten when the quota was not met.

Exodus 6.audience: The genealogy in this chapter traces the families of Levi, including Moses and Aaron and the Korahites (Exodus 6:16–25). Israel's priests and Levites knew these as their own family lines.

culture.title: Redeemer
culture.text: "I will redeem you" uses the language of family law: a kinsman redeemer bought back relatives sold into slavery or land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49).

culture.title: Uncircumcised lips
culture.text: Moses calls himself a man "of uncircumcised lips," using Israel's covenant sign as a figure for something unfit or not working properly—here, his speech.

Exodus 7.audience: Egypt's wealth came from the Nile. Israelite hearers knew it as the river that made Egypt a land of plenty, which makes its turning to blood a blow at the heart of Egypt's life.

culture.title: Egyptian magicians
culture.text: Egyptian priests and magicians served the court with rituals, spells, and interpretations. Paul names two of the magicians who opposed Moses as Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8).

culture.title: The Nile as god
culture.text: Egyptians honored the Nile's flood as the god Hapi, who brought fertility to the land.

Exodus 8.audience: Israel lived in Goshen, and the text notes that the flies did not come there (Exodus 8:22). Hearers would see the LORD distinguishing between Egypt and his people.

culture.title: Frogs
culture.text: Frogs bred in the Nile's marshes. The Egyptian goddess Heqet, associated with childbirth, was depicted with a frog's head.

culture.title: Sacrifices Egypt would despise
culture.text: Moses says Israel's sacrifices would be "the abomination of the Egyptians." Certain animals were sacred in Egyptian religion, so sacrificing them openly could provoke violence.

Exodus 9.audience: Livestock was wealth in the ancient world. Hearers would understand the scale of the loss when the plague on cattle, horses, donkeys, camels, oxen, and sheep struck Egypt (Exodus 9:3).

culture.title: Flax and barley
culture.text: The hail ruins the flax and barley, which ripen early, but not the wheat and rye (spelt), which ripen later. Flax was grown for linen, Egypt's main cloth.

culture.title: Furnace ashes
culture.text: Kilns and furnaces were used for making bricks and pottery. Moses throws furnace ashes into the air to bring boils on people and animals.

Exodus 10.audience: Locust swarms were a known disaster across the Near East (Joel 1:4). Hearers would understand that locusts arriving after the hail left nothing green in Egypt (Exodus 10:15).

culture.title: Darkness and the sun god
culture.text: The sun god Ra was among the most important gods of Egypt, and Pharaoh was called the son of Ra. Three days of darkness covered Egypt, while the Israelites had light in their homes.

culture.title: Feasts in the wilderness
culture.text: Moses insists that young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds must all go, "for we must hold a feast unto the LORD." Israel's later feasts included whole households (Deuteronomy 16:11).

Exodus 11.audience: Israel's law claimed every firstborn son and animal for the LORD, with firstborn sons redeemed (Exodus 13:2, 13). Hearers knew that custom as a memorial of the night described here.

culture.title: The firstborn
culture.text: The firstborn son held the place of heir and future head of the family. The plague reaches from Pharaoh's heir to the son of the maidservant at the hand-mill, the lowest servant.

culture.title: Grinding at the mill
culture.text: Grain was ground by hand between two stones, usually by women or servants. It was the most menial household task.

Exodus 12.audience: Israel kept the Passover every year as a memorial of this night (Exodus 12:14). Hearers knew its rules—the lamb, the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs—from their own celebrations.

culture.title: The month Abib
culture.text: This month becomes the first month of Israel's religious year. It falls in March–April, when barley ripens; it was called Abib (Exodus 13:4) and later Nisan (Esther 3:7).

culture.title: Unleavened bread
culture.text: Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept from a previous batch. Bread baked without it was quick to make. Israel ate unleavened bread because they left Egypt in haste.

culture.title: A mixed multitude
culture.text: People who were not Israelites left Egypt with them. Strangers could keep the Passover if they were circumcised (Exodus 12:48).

Exodus 13.audience: Israel's custom of redeeming every firstborn son, and its feast of unleavened bread, are explained here as memorials for later children who would ask what they mean (Exodus 13:14).

culture.title: Frontlets
culture.text: The text speaks of the exodus as "a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes." Later Jewish practice wore small boxes containing Scripture passages (phylacteries) on the arm and forehead (Matthew 23:5).

culture.title: The way of the Philistines
culture.text: The shortest route from Egypt to Canaan ran along the coast and was guarded by Egyptian forts. God leads Israel by another way so they will not face war at once.

Exodus 14.audience: The crossing of the sea was the event Israel celebrated above all others; psalms and prophets return to it again and again (Psalm 106:9–11; Isaiah 51:10).

culture.title: Chariots
culture.text: War chariots were the most advanced military weapon of the time. Egypt's chariot corps was its elite force; the text mentions six hundred chosen chariots.

culture.title: The Red Sea
culture.text: The Hebrew name is "Yam Suph," usually translated ‘sea of reeds.’ The exact place of the crossing is not known.

Exodus 15.audience: This is one of the oldest songs in Israel's worship. Hearers used it as a model of praise; Revelation describes the redeemed singing "the song of Moses" (Revelation 15:3).

culture.title: Women's victory songs
culture.text: After a victory, women led celebrations with tambourines (timbrels) and dancing, as Jephthah's daughter and the women of Israel did later (Judges 11:34; 1 Samuel 18:6).

culture.title: Bitter water
culture.text: Springs in the Sinai wilderness are often brackish or salty. Marah means ‘bitter.’ Elim, with twelve wells and seventy palm trees, was an oasis.

Exodus 16.audience: Israel kept a jar of manna before the LORD as a reminder for later generations (Exodus 16:32–34), and the Sabbath rest is first commanded here before the law at Sinai.

culture.title: An omer
culture.text: An omer was a dry measure, about two quarts (two liters). The text explains it as "the tenth part of an ephah" (Exodus 16:36).

culture.title: Quail
culture.text: Quail migrate across the Sinai region in large numbers each spring and autumn, often landing exhausted after crossing the sea.

Exodus 17.audience: The Amalekites were a desert people who remained Israel's enemies for generations—fought by Saul and David centuries later (1 Samuel 15; 30). This chapter records their first attack.

culture.title: Raising hands
culture.text: Raised hands were a posture of prayer and appeal to God (Psalm 28:2). Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' hands until sunset.

culture.title: Writing as a memorial
culture.text: This is the first time Scripture mentions writing in a book. Recording events in writing preserved them for later generations.

Exodus 18.audience: Israel's system of judges and elders later handled disputes at every level (Deuteronomy 1:15–17). This chapter describes how it began, on the advice of Moses' father-in-law.

culture.title: A priest of Midian
culture.text: Jethro was a priest in Midian, a people descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2). He offers sacrifices and eats with Israel's elders before God.

culture.title: Rulers of thousands
culture.text: Organizing people into units of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens was common in ancient armies and tribal societies. The same units appear in Israel's later military and civil leadership.

Exodus 19.audience: Israel heard this chapter as the moment they became a nation in covenant with the LORD, called "a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation" (Exodus 19:6).

culture.title: Covenant treaties
culture.text: Ancient Near Eastern treaties between a great king and a lesser people often began by recalling what the king had done for them, then set out obligations. God's words begin, "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians."

culture.title: Preparing to meet God
culture.text: The people wash their clothes, abstain from sexual relations, and stay off the mountain. Ritual purity was required for approaching what was holy.

Exodus 20.audience: The Ten Commandments were the heart of Israel's law, written on the tablets kept in the ark (Exodus 25:16; Deuteronomy 10:4–5). Every Israelite knew them.

culture.title: Images of gods
culture.text: Every nation around Israel worshipped gods through statues and images. Israel alone was forbidden to make any image to worship.

culture.title: Altars of earth and stone
culture.text: Altars were to be made of earth or uncut stones, without steps. Cut stone and steps were common in the temples of neighboring peoples.

Exodus 21.audience: These laws governed everyday life in Israel's villages. Hearers would know situations like these firsthand: debt servitude, injuries in quarrels, and goring oxen.

culture.title: Ancient law collections
culture.text: Other ancient peoples had written law codes, most famously the Code of Hammurabi of Babylon, which also includes the principle of "eye for eye." Such laws set a limit on punishment matching the injury.

culture.title: The goring ox
culture.text: An owner was responsible if he knew his ox was dangerous and did not keep it in. The Code of Hammurabi contains a similar law.

culture.title: Ear pierced at the door
culture.text: A servant who chose to stay with his master for life had his ear pierced with an awl against a doorpost, a public and permanent sign.

Exodus 22.audience: Israel's law repeatedly protects the widow, the fatherless, and the stranger (Exodus 22:21–24). Hearers knew these as the most vulnerable people in an agricultural society.

culture.title: Pledges and garments
culture.text: A poor man's outer cloak served as his blanket at night. If taken as a pledge for a loan, it had to be returned by sunset.

culture.title: Breaking in
culture.text: Houses were often built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through a wall. The KJV's "breaking up" describes this.

Exodus 23.audience: Israel's three yearly pilgrimage feasts are listed here (Exodus 23:14–17). Hearers knew them as the times when men went up to worship.

culture.title: Three harvest feasts
culture.text: Unleavened bread came at the barley harvest in spring, the feast of harvest (weeks) at the wheat harvest in early summer, and ingathering (tabernacles) at the fruit and grape harvest in autumn.

culture.title: Boiling a kid in its mother's milk
culture.text: This command is repeated three times in the law (also Exodus 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). Later Jewish practice built on it to keep meat and dairy apart.

culture.title: Leaving the land fallow
culture.text: Every seventh year the land was to rest, and the poor and wild animals could eat what grew. Leaving fields unplanted also allowed the soil to recover.

Exodus 24.audience: Israel's elders, priests, and people are all present for the ratifying of the covenant. Hearers knew this as the founding ceremony of their relationship with the LORD.

culture.title: Blood of the covenant
culture.text: Moses sprinkles half the blood on the altar and half on the people. Sharing blood bound both parties to the covenant. Jesus speaks of "the new testament in my blood" at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

culture.title: A covenant meal
culture.text: Treaties were often sealed with a shared meal. The elders "saw God, and did eat and drink."

Exodus 25.audience: Israel worshipped at the tabernacle, and later at the temple built on its pattern. Hearers knew these furnishings—the ark, the table, and the lampstand—as the objects at the center of their worship.

culture.title: Acacia wood
culture.text: Shittim (acacia) is a hard, durable tree that grows in the Sinai desert, one of the few sources of timber there.

culture.title: Portable sanctuaries
culture.text: Portable shrines carried on poles are known from Egypt, where sacred boats and chests were carried in processions. The ark's poles were never to be removed (Exodus 25:15).

culture.title: Showbread
culture.text: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were set out continually before the LORD and replaced every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–8).

Exodus 26.audience: Israelite hearers knew the layout described here: a holy place and a most holy place, divided by a veil. The temple Solomon built followed the same plan on a larger scale.

culture.title: Tent fabrics
culture.text: Linen, dyed wool of blue, purple, and scarlet, goat hair, and leather were the main tent materials. Purple dye, made from sea snails, was especially costly and associated with royalty.

culture.title: The veil
culture.text: The veil separated the holy place from the most holy, where only the high priest entered once a year (Leviticus 16:2). The Gospels record the temple veil torn when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51).

Exodus 27.audience: The bronze altar in the courtyard was where Israel's daily sacrifices were offered. Hearers knew the altar fire was to be kept burning.

culture.title: Horns of the altar
culture.text: Altars in the region often had raised corners called horns. Blood was put on them in sacrifice (Leviticus 4:7), and a person seeking protection might grasp them (1 Kings 1:50).

culture.title: Olive oil for light
culture.text: Lamps burned olive oil with a wick. "Pure oil olive beaten" was the finest grade, made by crushing olives rather than pressing them.

Exodus 28.audience: Israel's high priests wore these garments for centuries. Hearers knew the high priest by his breastplate with twelve stones, his ephod, and the gold plate reading "HOLINESS TO THE LORD" (Exodus 28:36).

culture.title: Engraved stones
culture.text: Engraving names on gemstones was a skilled craft, like cutting a seal. The high priest carried the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart.

culture.title: Urim and Thummim
culture.text: These were kept in the breastplate and used to seek God's decision (Numbers 27:21). Scripture does not describe exactly what they were or how they were used.

Exodus 29.audience: Israel's priests were set apart by this ordination ceremony, carried out later as described in Leviticus 8. Hearers knew that the daily morning and evening offering was made at the altar (Exodus 29:38–42).

culture.title: Anointing with oil
culture.text: Pouring oil on the head set a person apart for a special role. Priests, and later kings and some prophets, were anointed.

culture.title: Ear, thumb, and toe
culture.text: Blood was put on the priest's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. The same rite was used when a cleansed leper was restored (Leviticus 14:14).

Exodus 30.audience: Every Israelite man counted in a census paid the half-shekel ransom (Exodus 30:13). In Jesus' day a half-shekel temple tax was still collected each year (Matthew 17:24).

culture.title: Incense
culture.text: Incense was burned in temples across the ancient world. Israel's incense was a specific mixture of spices and frankincense, which was not to be copied for private use.

culture.title: The shekel of the sanctuary
culture.text: A shekel was a weight of silver, roughly two-fifths of an ounce (about 11 grams). The "shekel of the sanctuary" set the standard weight used at the tabernacle.

Exodus 31.audience: Israel's craftsmen are honored here: Bezaleel of Judah and Aholiab of Dan were filled with God's Spirit for skilled work. The chapter ends by restating the Sabbath as Israel's covenant sign.

culture.title: Skilled crafts
culture.text: Metalwork, gem cutting, and woodcarving were specialized trades passed down in families. Israel had learned such crafts in Egypt.

culture.title: Stone tablets
culture.text: Important laws and treaties were engraved on stone so they would last. The tablets were "written with the finger of God."

Exodus 32.audience: Israelite hearers knew that golden calves were later set up at Bethel and Dan by Jeroboam, with nearly the same words: "behold thy gods, O Israel" (1 Kings 12:28).

culture.title: Bulls as divine images
culture.text: Bulls symbolized strength and fertility across the ancient Near East. The Egyptian Apis bull was worshipped at Memphis, and Canaanite gods were linked with bulls.

culture.title: Smashing the tablets
culture.text: Breaking the tablets of a treaty was a sign that the agreement had been broken. Moses breaks them at the foot of the mountain.

Exodus 33.audience: The tent of meeting where the LORD spoke with Moses "face to face" (Exodus 33:11) was remembered in Israel as the place of Moses' unique closeness to God (Deuteronomy 34:10).

culture.title: Removing ornaments
culture.text: Taking off jewelry and finery was a sign of mourning and humility. The people strip off their ornaments after hearing God will not go up with them.

culture.title: Seeing a king's face
culture.text: In the ancient world, being admitted to a king's presence was a great privilege. God tells Moses, "there shall no man see me, and live."

Exodus 34.audience: The LORD's description of himself here—"merciful and gracious, longsuffering" (Exodus 34:6)—became one of the most quoted passages in Israel's Scriptures (Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Jonah 4:2).

culture.title: Asherah poles
culture.text: Groves in the KJV are Asherah poles—wooden objects honoring the Canaanite goddess Asherah—set up near altars. Israel was commanded to cut them down.

culture.title: A veil over Moses' face
culture.text: Moses' face shone after speaking with God, so he covered it with a veil when speaking to the people. Paul refers to this veil (2 Corinthians 3:13).

Exodus 35.audience: Israel's sanctuary was built from voluntary gifts. Hearers would note that men and women alike brought offerings and that women spun the goat hair and fine linen (Exodus 35:25–26).

culture.title: Spinning
culture.text: Spinning wool and flax into thread was mainly women's work in the ancient world, done by hand with a spindle.

culture.title: No fire on the Sabbath
culture.text: Lighting a fire meant gathering fuel and striking sparks—real labor in the ancient world. Israel was not to kindle fire on the Sabbath.

Exodus 36.audience: The people gave so much that Moses had to tell them to stop (Exodus 36:6–7). Hearers would contrast this with times when Israel's worship was neglected.

culture.title: Measurements and joinery
culture.text: Wooden frames were joined with tenons into silver sockets, so the structure could be taken apart and carried. The detailed measurements match the instructions given earlier in Exodus 26.

Exodus 37.audience: The ark, mercy seat, table, lampstand, and incense altar described here stood in the holy places of Israel's sanctuary. The temple in Jerusalem later held the ark in its most holy place (1 Kings 8:6).

culture.title: Gold overlay
culture.text: Covering wood with gold leaf or plating was a common technique for sacred objects in Egypt and the Near East, giving the appearance of solid gold with less metal.

culture.title: The almond-shaped lampstand
culture.text: The lampstand's cups were shaped like almond blossoms. The almond tree is the first tree to blossom in Israel's spring.

Exodus 38.audience: This chapter gives an account of the metals used in the tabernacle (Exodus 38:21–31). Hearers would recognize the bronze laver as a feature of their sanctuary.

culture.title: Bronze mirrors
culture.text: Mirrors in the ancient world were polished bronze or copper. The laver was made from mirrors given by the women who served at the door of the tabernacle.

culture.title: A talent
culture.text: A talent was the largest unit of weight, about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), equal to 3,000 shekels.

Exodus 39.audience: The phrase "as the LORD commanded Moses" repeats through this chapter. Israel's hearers would note that the priestly garments were made exactly as instructed.

culture.title: Gold thread
culture.text: Gold was beaten into thin plates and cut into wires to weave into fabric—an expensive craft known in Egypt for royal garments.

culture.title: Inspecting the work
culture.text: Moses inspects the finished work and blesses the people, as a master builder approved work done to plan.

Exodus 40.audience: The tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt (Exodus 40:17). Israel remembered the glory filling it, as it later filled Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11).

culture.title: Dedicating a sanctuary
culture.text: New temples in the ancient world were dedicated with ceremonies before use. The tabernacle and its furnishings are anointed with oil to make them holy.

culture.title: Travelling by the cloud
culture.text: Israel broke camp only when the cloud lifted from the tabernacle. Numbers 9:15–23 describes how this worked on the journey.
